title: What "Recursive" Adds: From Self-Refinement to RSI

questions.question: Which property separates a recursive self-improvement loop from ordinary self-refinement?
options: The system's benchmark score rises over several consecutive cycles
The system edits the mechanism that produces its next improvement
The system runs without a human reviewing each individual output
The system generates its own training data from its own outputs
questions.explanation: Shape (c) is recursive because the improver itself is edited, so the per-cycle gain becomes state. Rising scores, autonomy and self-generated data all occur in shapes (a) and (b) too.

questions.question: Shape (c) starts at C_0 = 1 with first gain g_0 = 0.3 and meta-gain r = 0.8. Where does it end up?
options: At 2.5x, the same ceiling a fixed improver with k = 0.2 reaches
At 4.0x, because the gains halve each cycle after the first one
At 1.3x, because only the first cycle's gain is ever realised
Nowhere finite, because any recursive loop grows without bound
questions.explanation: With r < 1 the gains form a geometric series: C = 1 + 0.3 / (1 - 0.8) = 2.5. A fixed improver with k = 1 - r = 0.2 and the same ceiling produces the identical sequence.

questions.question: main.py prints an identity check showing shape (a) and shape (c) with r = 0.8 agree to 1e-15. Why does that matter for classification?
options: It proves sub-critical recursion is just self-refinement, so the distinction can be dropped
It shows noise is required to tell the shapes apart, so --noise must always be set above zero
It shows the capability curve cannot reveal whether the improver was edited, so rungs come from the edit log
It shows a fixed improver always wins over 30 cycles when both ceilings are set to the same value
questions.explanation: Two loops with different structure produce the same numbers, so the rung must be read from what is edited and who applies it, which is why the 2026 ladders define levels that way.

questions.question: A system autonomously proposes patches to its own training harness, but an engineer must review and merge every patch. Where does Liu et al.'s ladder put it?
options: L4, because the improvement mechanism itself is what is being edited
L3, because the harness is an operational component and the loop validates
L5, because patches to a harness generalise across every task domain
L2, because humans still validate and apply the substantive changes
questions.explanation: Editing the mechanism does not reach L4 unless the system also applies and validates the edit itself; with a human in the apply step it is Assisted (L2). The classifier tests this boundary explicitly.

questions.question: ADAS's discovered agents transfer across domains and models, yet the classifier leaves it at L3. Why?
options: Its discovered agents transfer, but the meta agent that searches for them is never edited
Its verifier is an LLM judge, and judge-verified systems are capped at L3 by the criteria
It needs a human to seed the archive, which makes it assisted rather than programmatic
Its domain is a single benchmark family, so it cannot qualify as bounded RSI
questions.explanation: Generality without self-reference is not RSI: the L4 criterion is improving the improvement mechanism, and ADAS's meta agent stays fixed while the task agents it produces transfer.

questions.question: Why does this lesson insist that governance thresholds be defined on rungs rather than on impressions of a system?
options: Rungs are easier to explain to the public than benchmark scores and need no evaluation suite to be maintained
Benchmark jumps are an L3 trait and mechanism edits an L4 trait; a rung threshold fires on the second even if the score barely moves
Rung-based thresholds let a lab skip external evaluation because the level classification is self-reported
Rungs are defined by the papers' own claims, so a lab can rely on the authors' level assignment without checking
questions.explanation: The thresholds in RSP, PF and FSF are claims about who proposes, applies and validates and whether the mechanism is in scope. Read on attributes they are auditable; read on vibes they trigger on score jumps and miss mechanism edits.
